Project_Name: Tampa Bay Oil Spill - Boca Ciega Bay (Cross Bayou Mangrove Restoration)
Project_Description: The Cross Bayou site was planted as a salt marsh habitat with smooth cordgrass and will transition through natural processes into mangrove habitat.  The property has now been conveyed to Pinellas County for public recreation and conservation uses.
Restoration_Technique: contaminant removal/remediation, fill removal, invasives removal: vegetation, planting, stream channel reconnection/creation

Project_Name: Stony Coral Nurseries
Project_Description: This project utilizes volunteer groups, government, and academia to search for and recover viable loose corals or coral fragments from local reef areas, relocate them to a "nursery" or safe area, and monitor transplantation success and colony growth. Volunteer dive teams assist with coral collection, identification, transplantation, and monitoring. The long-term objective is to use coral colonies in the nursery for local coral reef habitat restoration projects.

Project_Name: Oleta River Wetland Restoration
Project_Description: This project restored a 30-acre wetland along the Oleta River. This consisted of removal of solid waste, soils and exotic vegetation, the placement of grading and fill, stabilization of the shoreline and the planting of native wetland vegetation.  Abandoned concrete structures such as seawalls and fill pads were removed, while the concrete debris was moved to the canal entrance. Mangroves were planted by volunteers in the final phase of restoration.
Restoration_Technique: debris removal, erosion control, fill removal, invasives removal: vegetation, planting
Lead_Implementer: Miami-Dade County Department of Environmental Resources Management

Project_Name: Tampa BayWatch Wetland Nursery Program
Project_Description: NOAA's Community-based Restoration Program, Restore America's Estuaries, and Fish America Foundation partnered with Tampa Bay Watch to fund the Tampa Bay High School Wetland Nursery Program to restore mangroves and salt marshes. High school ecology and science club students built wetland nurseries on campus and grew salt marshes to be used for Tampa Bay restoration projects. As many as 300 community volunteers joined the students to participate in weekend planting events. In a typical year, an average of 20,000 salt marsh plants may be transplanted to restore an average of 5 acres or more of habitat.

Project_Name: Blind Creek Park Restoration
Project_Description: NOAA's Community-Based Restoration Program and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service provided partial funding for the removal of Australian pines in the 2-mile dune restoration at Blind Creek Park on South Hutchinson Island, St. Lucie County, Florida. The presence of non-native Australian pines in the park has resulted in increased erosion and reduced nesting areas for several species of endangered and threatened sea turtles. The roots act as a physical barrier for Green, Leatherback, and Loggerhead turtles trying to excavate nesting sites. Approximately 1.5 miles of the 2-mile project were cleared of Australian pine and approximately 25 acres of native dune vegetation was planted by community volunteers.
Restoration_Technique: culvert modification (including replacement), culvert removal, debris removal, invasives removal: vegetation, planting
Lead_Implementer: St. Lucie County Mosquito Control District

Project_Name: Pepper Buster and Johnny Mangrove Seed
Project_Description: The Brazilian pepper plant is an extremely adaptive plant that was introduced to Florida as an ornamental shrub and has since invaded and replaced native mangrove and upland habitat in the Indian River Lagoon. This project restored areas in Indian River Lagoon by removing Brazilian pepper and replanting native shoreline vegetation.  A total of seven acres was restored. In addition, the funds received for the project supported the development of a field restoration manual for distribution to other volunteer groups throughout Florida.

Project_Name: Mangrove Marsh Impoundment Habitat Restoration
Project_Description: Since the 1950s, more than 40,000 acres of Florida salt and mangrove marsh habitat has been diked off and flooded to prevent mosquitoes from laying their eggs in the mud.  In order to improve tidal flow and habitat for fish within an 18-acre diked section of mangrove marsh, the old berms were removed and a connection to the Indian River Lagoon was reestablished.

Project_Name: Pepper Cove Impoundment Restoration
Project_Description: This project reconnects an historic salt marsh to the Indian River Lagoon and includes the removal of exotic Brazilian pepper trees and the installation of two culverts.  Replanting of the marsh will occur after the impoundment stabilizes and acclimates.
Restoration_Technique: culvert modification (including replacement), invasives removal: vegetation, planting
Lead_Implementer: Brevard County Environmentally Endangered Lands (EEL) Program

Project_Name: Voyager Grounding Site Restoration
Project_Description: Frequent small vessel groundings are having significant cumulative effects on coral reefs. This project developed a Reef Medic program to help prevent boat groundings, report them when they occur, and help repair grounding sites. Objectives of the Reef Medic program include: 1) training volunteers to assist staff with restoration of small vessel grounding sites, 2) fostering community awareness, participation, and stewardship of natural resources, and 3) using an existing grounding site as a training site for Reef Medic volunteers.
Restoration_Technique: coral reattachment, debris removal, rubble stabilization
Lead_Implementer: Mote Marine Laboratory Pigeon Key Marine Research Center
Species_Benefited: (Coral, boulder star - Threatened), (Coral, mountainous star - Candidate), (Sea fan, common)

Project_Name: Waste Tire Removal for Reef Fish Habitat Restoration
Project_Description: In 1967, Florida began building artificial reefs with waste tires. Over the years, many of the tires have washed ashore and continue to move around due to wave action and currents.  Near Fort Lauderdale, numerous tires have being forced up against the eastern edge of the middle coral reef. This project removed and recycled those waste tires from a section of natural coral reef off of Fort Lauderdale. Eighty-eight volunteer divers completing a total of 158 dives and successfully removed 1,600 tires that covered approximately 20 square meters of sea-bottom.

Project_Name: Egret Island Restoration
Project_Description: Funding provided by the NOAA Restoration Center Community-based Restoration Program, the Fish America Foundation, the Nature Conservancy, and Monroe County was used to restore Egret Island, Florida and the adjacent tidal creek to its original habitat of tropical hardwood hammock, coastal wetlands, and tidal creek/seagrass beds. A bridge connecting the island to Key Largo was removed to enhance tidal flushing. Egret Island is a small coastal island located in the John Pennekamp Coral Reef State Park in Key Largo, Florida and is the most visited park in the Florida State Park system.

In addition, Tampa Bay Watch, along with students from Bloomingdale and Countryside High Schools, and community volunteers supported the restoration project by assisting in the planting of approximately 500 mangroves and 2,700 salt marsh units.

The planting of native vegetation will occur subsequent to exotic removal.

Project_Name: Tarpon Key Salt Marsh Restoration

This program restored 2.5 acres of salt marsh on Tarpon Key, a mangrove island near the mouth of Tampa Bay. 55 Pinellas County students transplanted 4,000 school-grown saltmarsh units to an eroding shoreline area along the western face of the sanctuary. Project_Name: Ft. DeSoto Monitoring Project
Project_Description: The Ft. DeSoto Monitoring Project implemented pre and post-construction monitoring to capture the effects of re-opening tidal connections that were closed during the 1950s and 1960s in the back bays of Mullet Key.  The historic tidal connections were lost by the construction of a man-made causeway, but were reestablished in 2004 by installing a bridge to restore circuitous tidal flow.  Data from seagrass samples, water quality samples, sediment cores, and temperature loggers, etc. were all collected to document the benefit of this project on the Ft. DeSoto ecosystem.

Project_Name: Green Shores Oyster Reef and Saltmarsh Creation
Project_Description: NOAA’s Community-Based Restoration Program partnered with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation, the Florida Department of Environmental Protection, the United States Navy, Fish America Foundation, the Nature Conservancy, and others to construct an oyster reef breakwater from limestone rock and oyster shell and create an intertidal salt marsh area behind the reef in a 15 acre area of Pensacola Bay. The shoreline along Bayfront Parkway in downtown Pensacola, Florida has been heavily impacted by human activities. Local volunteers, students, local restaurants, and oyster bars stockpiled oyster shell for the project. Volunteers planted native emergent marsh vegetation, while scientists planted seagrasses. The restoration site is already highly productive, hosting up to 800 birds a day as well as many marine fish and invertebrates.
Restoration_Technique: oyster reef construction, placement of fill/dredge material, planting

Project_Name: Matheson Hammock Tidal Flow Restoration
Project_Description: Matheson Hammock County Park, a 832-acre park in Dade County, Florida, was devastated in 1992 by Hurricane Andrew. The park's previously functioning mangrove ecosystem was severely impacted by the storm due to fallen tree debris that has clogged the tidal corridors, preventing flushing. The Wildlife Research Team (WRT) restored this mangrove habitat by unclogging the tidal creeks and removing debris in cross corridors.  WRT volunteers used canoes to carefully remove dead and decayed flora, including both above and below water remains of large red and black mangrove trees and invasive, non-native species such as Australian pine. WRT’s efforts were funded by grants from NOAA's Community-Based Restoration Program, in partnership with the Fish America Foundation.

Project_Name: Hobe Sound Mangrove Wetlands Restoration - Phase 1
Project_Description: As part of a larger effort to reverse coastal wetland habitat loss and removal of invasive species adjacent to the Indian River Lagoon (IRL), MRC will educate local residents and supervise them in hands-on shoreline restoration activities.  Activities will include invasive species removal and planting native species such as mangroves.  The target area for this project is the IRL with special emphasis on the Hobe Sound National Wildlife Refuge and 46 acres of adjacent public conservation lands known as Bonair Beach.  These lands make up a 2000 acre greenway encompassing over seven miles of barrier island with continuous IRL shoreline.

Project_Name: Ft. DeSoto Tidal Flow Restoration
Project_Description: Through funding from NOAA’s Restoration Center, in partnership with the US Fish and Wildlife Foundation, the Pinellas County Environmental Foundation, and others, volunteers constructed a bridge to restore circulation to the back bays of Mullet Key in Ft. DeSoto Park, Florida. Tidal flow between bays in the Fort DeSoto Park Aquatic Habitat Management Area in Pinellas County were severed during the dredging and filling activities that occurred in the late 1950s.  Summertime temperatures become extremely elevated in these areas leading to very low dissolved oxygen levels as well as severe seagrass stress. Restored circulation has improved water quality healthier essential fish habitat. Fish and crabs had migrated into the area within a few days.
Restoration_Technique: berm/dike removal, planting, tide gate modification (including replacement)

Tidal flow between bays in the Fort DeSoto Park Aquatic Habitat Management Area in Pinellas County were severed during the dredging and filling activities that occurred in the late 1950s.  Summertime temperatures become extremely elevated in these areas leading to very low dissolved oxygen levels as well as severe seagrass stress. Restored circulation has improved water quality healthier essential fish habitat. Fish and crabs had migrated into the area within a few days.
Restoration_Technique: berm/dike removal, planting, tide gate modification (including replacement)

Project_Description: A study of seagrass restoration in Tampa Bay, FL was undertaken to compare the relative success of seagrass restoration conducted using three different types of planting methods or designs including large clumped, small clumped and small spaced techniques. Project_Name: Environmental Distance Learning Project
Project_Description: The Environmental Distance Learning Program is an on-line service designed to provide real time environmental information to educators and students of Pinellas County, Florida. This program is a web-based environmental distance learning system that connects students and educators to their environment through a network of watershed sensors. This project was funded to eventually guide applications of the program outside of Pinellas County.

Project_Name: Tampa Bay Seagrass Restoration Strategy
Project_Description: The Tampa Bay Seagrass Strategy used a comprehensive ten part approach to identify the factors limiting successful restoration of seagrass along the western shore of Old Tampa Bay. Based on these applied research results, project partners ranging from seagrass restoration scientists to resource managers defined specific actions needed to encourage seagrass recovery in these areas and then explained them to the community. This project has provided a great foundation of information that will help spur on future restoration efforts.

Project_Name: Tampa Bay Oil Spill - Boca Ciega Bay (Turtle Crawl Point Saltmarsh Planting)
Project_Description: To compensate the public for injuries to saltmarsh vegetation resulting from the 1993 Tampa Bay oil spill, the responsible party was required to plant approximately 7,260 planting units of smooth cordgrass, Spartina alterniflora, at Turtle Crawl Point at the Pinellas County War Veterans Memorial Park.  Nursery grown 2" peatpots of smooth cordgrass was planted in areas that, at the time of the planting effort, did not support any vegetation.  The responsible party was required to plant approximately 1.5 acres of unvegetated habitat.

Project_Name: Tampa Bay Oil Spill - Boca Ciega Bay (Bird Island Salt Marsh Planting)
Project_Description: Smooth cordgrass, Spartina alterniflora, planting units were installed at Bird Island to provide compensatory restoration for injuries to saltmarsh habitat resulting from the 1993 Tampa Bay oil spill.  The responsible party hired a contractor, Lewis Environemntal Services, Inc. who then purchases and installed 100 planting units.

Project_Name: Tampa Bay Oil Spill - City of St. Pete Beach (7th Avenue Fishing Pier)
Project_Description: The project involved rehabilitation of the fishing pier which previously existed at 7th Avenue and Pass a Grille Way in the City of St. Pete Beach.

Project_Name: Tampa Bay Oil Spill - City of St. Pete Beach (Blind Pass Park Fishing Pier)
Project_Description: The project involved the construction of a new fishing pier at the public park at 9300 Blind Pass Road, Blind Pass Park.  This project will compensate the public for the lost use of waterways for recreation during the 1993 oil spill by providing increased access to recreational anglers who fish in Blind Pass.

Project_Name: Tampa Bay Oil Spill - City of St. Pete Beach (Gulf Way Walkway)
Project_Description: This walkway project will compensate the public for the loss of recreational use of area beaches during the 1993 Tampa Bay oil spill.  The Gulf Way Beach Walkway project in Passe-a-Grille is a concrete walkway that ties into a previously existing beach walkway system and extends the existing walkway system to the north from 9th Avenue to 23rd Avenue, approximately 3400 feet.  The walkway is of similar  design and width to the existing walkway.  The project will enhance public access to the beach and provide greater opportunity for passive and active use of the beach.

Project_Name: Tampa Bay Oil Spill - City of St. Pete Beach (E 33rd Ave Boat Ramp)
Project_Description: The Trustee Council for the 1993 Tampa Bay oil spill selected one project to compensate the public's lost use of area waterways.  The project replaced the City of St. Pete Beach boat ramp near the Don Cesar Hotel.  This public boat ramp was deteriorating and in need of major rehabilitation.  Boat owners risked damage to their trailers if they use the ramp in its previous condition.  The project involved replacing the cement boat ramp with a pre-fabricated ramp, featuring a non-slip surface.  Replacement of this ramp ensures and encourages continued use of this ramp to access area waters for recreational boating and fishing.

Project_Name: Tampa Bay Oil Spill - City of Madeira Beach (Shoreline Park)
Project_Description: A project providing for development of the Madeira Beach Causeway Shoreline Restoration Park was selected for funding by the Trustee Council for the Tampa Bay oil spill. This project will compensate the public for lost use of area shorelines and waterways for recreation during the spill. The project incorporates a number of features primarily intended to encourage and support a variety of passive recreational activities at this site. The project includes boardwalks that take visitors through connecting outdoor interpretive and educational displays along the park's shoreline.  The project also restored some oyster habitat along the shoreline.  Finally, the project establishes some other native vegetation throughout the site such as live oaks and cabbage palms.  Development of the park represents a new access to natural resources and new recreational amenities for the public.

Project_Name: Tampa Bay Oil Spill - City of Indian Rocks Beach (Central Ave Beach Access)
Project_Description: The project includes the construction of a new dune walkover and four marine sensitive lighting bollards.

Project_Name: Tampa Bay Oil Spill - City of Indian Rocks Beach (Nature Preserve Boardwalk)
Project_Description: The Trustee Council for the Tampa Bay oil spill selected to fund the construction of a boardwalk through a public nature preserve owned by the City of Indian Rocks Beach to compensate the public's loss of use of natural resources during the spill and subsequent cleanup.  The boardwalk meanders through mangrove habitat and terminates on the open water of the intracoastal waterway.  The boardwalk is over 1000 feet long with connecting loops and several benches along its length.

Existing dune crossovers, in need of repair or replacement, was removed and new, higher and wider crossovers were constructed.  The higher crossovers allow for the formation of more stable, protective dune habitat at these locations.  Replacement of the degraded boardwalks also creates a safer access point for pedestrians, including those with physical disabilities

Project_Description: The Trustees considered and selected two major walkways in Treasure Island as a single project. Project_Description: This project includes a new boardwalk at a Pinellas County park to compensate the public for lost recreational access to area waterways during the 1993 Tampa Bay oil spill. Project_Name: Fantasy Island Salt Marsh and Oyster Restoration
Project_Description: The Coastal Conservation Association of Florida has partnered with Tampa Bay Watch, the Florida Aquarium, and local Boy Scout troops to create a series of new oyster bars at Fantasy Island and Green Key. The oyster reef will help prevent shoreline erosion, provide hard bottom habitat, and improve water quality in the Tampa Bay estuary. In addition, 40 sixth graders, their parents, teachers and volunteers planted 5,000 plugs of salt marsh grasses along one acre of shoreline. A second planting added 2,000 plugs of smooth cordgrass. NOAA's Community-based Restoration Program and the Fish America Foundation provided partial funding to support this project.

Project_Name: Green Key Oyster Restoration
Project_Description: Green Key is a small island located near the mouth of the Alafia River in an area of Tampa Bay, FL commonly referred to as the Kitchen. This project created of a series of oyster bars was in an effort to prevent further erosion, create habitat, improve water quality, and buffer the area from wave action, providing optimal conditions for the settlement of salt marsh plants and mangroves. Five oyster bars were installed on Green Key in two events. In all, 24 tons of fossilized oyster shell was deposited on the shoreline of Green Key. After 24 months, the created reefs have excellent oyster growth and appear to be healthy. Funding was provided through NOAA's Community-based Restoration Program partnership with the Fish America Foundation.

Project_Name: Indian River Lagoon Salt Marsh Nursery
Project_Description: The Orlando Chapter of Coastal Conservation Association of Florida, with the help of volunteers, created two smooth cordgrass nurseries, renovated an existing red mangrove greenhouse, and used red mangroves and smooth cordgrass grown in the nurseries to restore and enhance contiguous and spoil island shorelines in the Indian River Lagoon. Goals of the project included planting 20,000 red mangrove propagules at four different sites and planting 1,000 smooth cordgrass sprigs at one site.

Project_Name: Tampa Bay Oil Spill - Eleanor Island Emergency Stabilization (Oyster Restoration)
Project_Description: The project was an emergency restoration action to restore oyster reef including removing contaminated oyster shell and oil mats, replacing with fossil oyster shell to stablize the remaining oyster beds and mangrove fringe and facilitating oyster recolonization.

Project_Name: Florida Keys Diadema antillarum Restoration
Project_Description: This project explored the optimum habitat and size for release and grow-out of Diadema antillarum.  Teams introduced wild and lab-reared Diadema to coral reef sites selected based on low coral coverage and high algal coverage.  It was anticipated that the Diadema would  then graze on the algae, thus providing increased area for new coral recruits.  TNC staff and volunteers monitored Diadema survivability and changes to the benthic community caused by Diadema grazing.  Grazed-down substrate was also seeded with cultured coral larvae in order to enhance coral recruitment.

Project_Name: Tampa BayWatch Brazilian Pepper Eradication
Project_Description: Through a grant provided by NOAA's Community-based Restoration Program and Restore America's Estuaries, Tampa Bay Watch and 175 college students from around the country and staff from Hillsborough County cut down 2-3 acres of Brazilian pepper. Brazilian peppers in the Tampa Bay area are displacing mangrove forests at an alarming rate, which in turn is reducing vital coastal habitat for native wildlife. The stumps were treated with herbicide and the area was replanted with native vegetation to prevent regrowth.

Project_Name: Recording Manatee Movements in Tampa Bay
Project_Description: Research using state-of-the-art GPS equipment and data loggers (Argos-linked GPS and time-depth-temperature data loggers) was coupled with an ongoing project entitled, "Calibrating Manatee Aerial Survey Counts at Tampa Bay Power Plants in Winter."   The primary objective of this study was to obtain detailed information on manatee movements around Tampa Bay power plants that allows researchers and natural resource managers to understand how manatees are using these warm-water sites.  Identification of these important habitats is critical to the long term protection and conservation of manatees and their habitats.
Lead_Implementer: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission

The effort resulted in the salvage and reattachment of over 125 coral fragments ranging in size from a few inches to a large 600+ pound Montastrea coral estimated to be over 150 years old.

The tabloid empowers students and teachers to investigate water quality issues in their own communities and take action to improve and protect water resources.

Project_Name: Juvenile Red Drum Habitat Identification

Information from this study is a valuable contribution to Tampa Bay fisheries management and habitat conservation efforts.

Project_Description: This project researched and created an oyster restoration mat technique that will be effective for shallow water, intertidal oyster reefs in areas with intense boating activity.  This project involved high school and university students in collecting materials, building shell restoration mats, deploying mats, and monitoring oyster recruitment.

Project_Name: Canaveral Tidal Pool Park
Project_Description: This project restored mangrove and saltmarsh grass habitat along 5,200 linear feet of shoreline at Port Canaveral.  Restoration activities included planting 250 black mangrove seedlings, 20,000 rooted red mangrove propagules, and 4,000 smooth cordgrass sprigs. They also built a second nursery at Titusville High School. Approximately 30-acres of native vegetation was restored and the site now provides a source of increased recreational and educational opportunities for the community.

Project_Description: This site's marine habitat has been restored by building a large artificial reef using 100 reef balls, cement structures designed to provide fish and shellfish habitat. The activities enhanced the population of reef fish by establishing a marine hardbottom habitat.

Project_Name: Lemon Bay Preserve Habitat Restoration
Project_Description: Over 15 acres of coastal wetlands were restored with the help of volunteers. Volunteers conducted exotic plant removal efforts, fish and wildlife surveys and water quality monitoring. They also planted thousands of native species, including salt marsh cordgrass, black needlerush, and mangroves.

Project_Name: A.J. Palonis Park Oyster Restoration
Project_Description: Tampa Bay Watch in partnership with the Coastal Conservation Association of Florida and local community groups created a series of new oyster bars and planted salt marsh habitat at A.J. Palonis Jr. Park in Tampa Bay. Oyster shell material was placed on the tidal flats to create oyster reefs at five sites within the park and salt marsh vegetation was planted on the shoreline behind the new oyster reefs in an effort to restore lost habitat, prevent further erosion of shorelines and improve water quality through natural filtration. A total of 153 volunteers contributed 624 hours to place nearly 40 tons of shell in the restoration site. Funding for this project was provided by the NOAA Restoration Center's Community-based Restoration Program and Fish America Foundation.

Project_Name: Davis Tract Salt Marsh Restoration
Project_Description: This project has enhanced fisheries in Tampa Bay by restoring and creating 7 acres of coastal wetland habitat. It has provided environmental education outreach and hands-on volunteer planting opportunities for the community.

Project_Name: Florida Monitoring of Exotics in Ballast Water
Project_Description:
The goal of this project is to compile a comprehensive inventory of the existing microorganisms in the water and sediments in Tampa Bay and to sample ballast waters from ships entering the Tampa Bay Port.  Ships are known to act as vectors for the transfer of toxic and harmful microorganisms via ballast water discharges into ports and harbors.

This project successfully sampled the ballasts of foreign vessels entering the Port of Tampa along with local sediment and water and tested for water-borne or sediment-residing life stages of harmful microalgae.  Additionally, the project successfully modified the sampling protocols for testing for microalgae in Tampa.  A 151-page report was completed detailing the issue of "ballast Water as an Accidental Vector for the Introduction of Harmful Microalgae Species into Tampa Bay, FL."
Lead_Implementer: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission

Project_Name: Upper Boca Ciega Bay Oyster Reef Monitoring
Project_Description: This effort acted as a companion restoration project to the oyster monitoring component funded through DARRP as part of Tampa Bay Oil Spill restoration funds.  The objective of this project was to conduct applied research on an oyster reef constructed with different substrates of fresh shell and fossilized shell.  In addition, the project assisted with the establishment of a pilot shell recycling program within the community to be used for future oyster reef restoration projects in Tampa Bay.

Project_Name: Howard Park Beach Sea Oats Planting
Project_Description: This project stabilized the coast and has prevented erosion along a 5 acre stretch at Fred Howard Park in Tarpon Springs, Florida by the planting of 10,000 Sea Oats. It incorporated school and community groups in the restoration activities.

Project_Name: Bayside Field Studies
Project_Description: This project allowed the Florida Aquarium to develop and deliver a comprehensive environmental education program on the Tampa Bay Watershed for high school marine science and biology students and their teachers.  Participants were involved with a variety of hands-on activities focused on Tampa Bay's aquatic habitats.

Project_Name: Florida Pectinid Workshop
Project_Description: This workshop, hosted by the University of South Florida in 2003, provided a unique opportunity for researchers in scallop biology, aquaculture practitioners, and conservation managers to present their most recent findings to their peers. The information obtained through this workshop has been beneficial to the restoration of bay scallops in Tampa Bay.

Project_Name: Clear Creek Gully Restoration Project
Project_Description: Clear Creek, located in Northwest Florida, is a small stream located near a historic borrow pit.  The borrow pit had evolved into a 45-acre gully that poured massive amounts of sediment into Clear Creek and eventually into the Blackwater River and Blackwater Bay, which was affecting the migration of gulf sturgeon.  This project  stabilized the pit by creating a new stream channel in the bottom of the borrow pit.  The riparian floodplain was planted with native vegetation to stabilize the stream banks. Some isolated wetlands were created to handle excessive flows from secondary gullies.  Additionally, offsite stormwater retention was constructed to limit high discharge and shear stress into the gully and new stream channel.
Restoration_Technique: planting, storm water/runoff controls, stream channel reconnection/creation
Lead_Implementer: Three River Resource Conservation and Development Council Inc.

Project_Name: Ft.Pickens/St.Andrews Aquatic Preserves Prop Scar Restoration
Project_Description: The Fort Pickens and St. Andrews Aquatic Preserves, near Pensacola, Florida, have accumulated a high density of prop scars in seagrass beds, mainly from recreational boating. This project repaired prop scar damage and reduced future damage to the area by transplanting grass plugs from donor beds to the scarred area. The project also raised public awareness and tested methods for use with damaged seagrass beds elsewhere in Northwest Florida.
Lead_Implementer: Florida Department of Environmental Protection Coastal and Aquatic Managed Areas

Project_Name: Tarpon Bay Hydrologic Restoration
Project_Description: In the 1950s and 1960s, a road was constructed connecting a small group of islands called the Isles of Capri in Collier County. The road was designed without any culverts or bridges and consequently halted all tidal flushing and water transport between the islands. This caused silt to build up in two major bay systems, Johnson Bay and Tarpon Bay, resulting in poor water quality and severe degradation of important nursery and estuarine habitat. This project restored natural tidal flow between the two bays by installing a box culvert through an existing causeway.
Species_Benefited: (Crab, blue), (Crab, stone), (Drum, red), (Ladyfish), (Manatee, west indian - Range-wide - Endangered), (Mullet, striped), (Seatrout, spotted), (Snook)

Project_Name: Invasive Marine Species Workshop Sponsorship
Project_Description: Grant money was used to host a workshop on marine invasive species found in Florida's saltwater systems. The workshop synthesized the current understanding of invasive species and then identified and prioritized scientific and educational questions about these species. The title of the workshop was "Invasive Species in Florida's Saltwater Systems: Where we are and where we're going".

Project_Description: The objective of this project is to monitor the constructed oyster reef for settlement stability, fish utilization, and beneficial effects of the reef on the adjacent seagrass community. Project_Description: The Marine Resources Council, in partnership with the Florida Department of Environmental Protection, and with the help of volunteers restored approximately 230 acres of shoreline through invasive species removal and native mangrove planting. Site locations extend throughout the San Sebastian River State Buffer Preserve, the Sebastian Inlet State Park and the Pelican Island National Wildlife Refuge.

Project_Description: NOAA's Community-based Restoration Program, Restore America's Estuaries and Fish America Foundation partnered with Tampa Bay Watch to fund salt marsh restoration at multiple sites around Tampa Bay.  High school ecology and science club students built on-campus wetland nurseries to grow salt marsh grasses for Tampa Bay restoration efforts. Project_Name: Fort Brooke Salt Marsh Restoration

High school ecology and science club students built on-campus wetland nurseries to grow salt marsh grasses for Tampa Bay restoration efforts. This program restored salt marsh at Fort Brooke near Tampa Bay, Florida. The site was restored through cooperation with the City of Tampa and the Southwest Florida Water Management District. Volunteers planted 2,500 smooth cordgrass units to restore the salt marsh and upland vegetation was  incorporated into the project. The site will ultimately be used as an urban park.

Project_Name: Ulu May Sanctuary Shoreline Habitat Restoration
Project_Description: The Ulu May Wildlife Sanctuary is a natural lagoon surrounded by a man-made dike linked to canals originally created for mosquito control.   This wildlife reserve has become home to the Brazilian pepper plant, an invasive species that has caused a domino effect of events.  Brazilian pepper trees have overrun the shoreline and killed off native plants destroying important fish nursery habitat.  In addition, the mangrove population has been decimated by this plant which has had a detrimental effect on the stability of shoreline sediment. Keep Brevard Beautiful, in partnership with the FishAmerica Foundation, the NOAA Restoration Center, and local volunteers eradicated invasive Brazilian Pepper trees from 33 acres of the Ulu May Sanctuary.

Project_Name: Wonderful Water Exhibit
Project_Description: Great Explorations, Inc. designed, developed and built an interactive exhibit to help children and adults realize the vital importance of water resources. The Wonderful Water Exhibit focused on water systems, water quality, conservation, alternative water sources, and flood protection.

Project_Name: Pinellas County Adopt-A-Pond Pilot Project
Project_Description: The Pinellas County Adopt-A-Pond Pilot Project is an integrated approach to educating and training homeowners to restore and maintain their stormwater ponds to improve water quality, reduce run-off, and enhance wildlife habitat by removing invasive vegetation and replanting with native species. This has contributed to an overall improvement of water quality in Pinellas County.

Project_Name: Clam Bayou Restoration Project
Project_Description: Through a cooperative approach of multiple partners such as the J.N 'Ding' Darling National Wildlife Refuge, the US Fish and Wildlife Service, the South Florida Water Management District, and local homeowner's associations, the NOAA Community-based Restoration Program awarded $100,000 in funding to restore tidal flushing between Clam Bayou and Dinkins Bayou, Florida. Project_Name: Terra Ceia Upland Habitat Restoration
Project_Description: This project restored 217 acres of coastal pine flatwoods and hammocks within the Terra Ceia Aquatic and Buffer Preserve.  In this area, the majority of coastal uplands had been previously cleared and ditched for agricultural use.  The culmination of these practices left the site dominated by exotic species.  This project  removed the invasive species and then replanted the site with native upland vegetation.  This effort fits into a greater habitat restoration master plan for the Preserve.

Project_Name: Tampa Shoreline Restoration Initiative
Project_Description: The Tampa Shoreline Restoration Initiative was a collaborative project of the Mayor's Beautification Program and multiple Tampa Bay stakeholders to restore the shoreline along 30 City owned public open spaces.  This Initiative created a restoration master plan for the City which then led an extensive public outreach campaign to recruit volunteers.  Volunteers participated in all 39 restoration work days ranging from invasive species removal efforts to native planting events.

Project_Name: Davis Tract Oyster Restoration

Tampa BayWatch is working with both groups to permit five new shell bars in the largest tidal pond on the northeastern corner of the restoration project.  The new oyster bars will be built with shell bags to prevent shell migration.  Two separate 100 foot reefs will be built.

Project_Name: Bayshore Boulevard Oyster Habitat and Salt Marsh Restoration
Project_Description: In order restore hard bottom and provide habitat suitable for oyster larvae settlement and growth, Tampa Bay Watch administers an oyster dome program. Project_Name: Davis Island Salt Marsh Restoration
Project_Description: Tampa Bay Watch works with local schools to develop and maintain salt marsh grass nurseries.  Students at Dowdell Middle School transplanted approximately 2,000 saltmarsh plants to the Davis Island Boat Basin to restore approximately 0.5 acres of tidal wetland.  Florida Aquarium campers also contributed to the effort by planting an additional 0.5 acres.

Project_Name: Saltern Restoration Effects at Weedon Island Preserve
Project_Description: This three year project 'Monitoring the Effects of Saltern Restoration at Weedon Island Preserve' had 3 major objectives: (1) to evaluate the effectiveness of a saltern/mangrove restoration project using a newly developed restoration technique,  (2) compare floral and faunal use in saltern/mangrove systems versus solely mangrove habitat, and (3) to develop a brochure on salterns regarding their contribution to an estuarine landscape.  Results from the study indicated that saltern habitat interspersed with mangroves provides edge habitat that favors a greater assemblage of species.  In addition, the study highlighted that the berm blasting saltern restoration technique does not appear to restore the site to the appropriate elevations and needs to be further refined.
Lead_Implementer: Preserving the Environment through Ecological Research (PEER)

Project_Name: Manatee Viewing Center Invasive Plant Removal Project
Project_Description: The Invasive Species Plant Task Force, a partnership of local, county, and state government representatives as well as private industry and community organizations, implemented an upland restoration project at Sun City Heritage Park along the Manatee River.  This project resulted in the restoration of 9.5 acres of upland habitat cleared of invasive plant species allowing for the successful recruitment of native species.  Three volunteer events were held to help remove invasive/exotic Brazilian pepper, lead tree and air potato species and the efforts of this project benefited the entire 28-acre footprint of the park.
Lead_Implementer: Hillsborough County Parks, Recreation and Conservation

Project_Name: Wall Springs Park Ecosystem Restoration
Project_Description: The 'Wall Springs Park Ecosystem Restoration Project' restored a mosaic of habitats across the 195-acre site.  Upland, mangrove, freshwater wetland, sandhill, pine flatwoods, and saltmarsh habitat all benefited from the completion of this project.  Invasive exotic plant species were removed through the use of mechanical cutting, chipping and grinding, and herbicidal treatment.  Interpretive signage was also installed on site to help educate and  inform park visitors about the negative impacts of invasive plants and how to identify invasive species.

Project_Name: Tampa Bay Stewardship Initiative
Project_Description: The 'Tampa Bay Stewardship Initiative - Phase I", implemented by Tampa Bay Watch, completed several individual projects to help protect, conserve, and restore the natural resources of Tampa Bay.  From the spring of 2004 to the fall of 2006  Tampa Bay Watch completed a scallop restoration and monitoring program including the Great Bay Scallop Search, helped to protect the colonial bird nesting islands through nine clean-up events, hosted 5 derelict crab trap removal events, and enhanced their education and monitoring program through  curriculum development, teacher education, and the formation of an Education Advisory Council.
Species_Benefited: (Crab, blue), (Crab, stone), (Grass, turtle), (Pelican, brown - Endangered), (Scallop, bay)

Project_Name: Global Rivers Environmental Education Network (GREEN) Youth Program
Project_Description: The Suncoast Earth Force GREEN program is an educational initiative to help teachers and students connect with their watersheds. Through a service learning approach, students were taught how to identify environmental issues in their own communities and put their knowledge to work by implementing hands-on environmental projects in the Tampa Bay watershed.

Project_Name: Discovery Garden Environmental Landscape Education and Demonstration Project
Project_Description: The Hillsborough County Extension Service's horticulture outreach is focused on the Florida Yards and Neighborhoods (FYN) Program.  This project took the concepts of the FYN program and created the Discovery Garden to provide a demonstration site for landscape design and maintenance practices that lessen the impacts on water quality and the environment.  The site demonstrating various types of pervious surfaces, combined with educational workshops, pamphlets, videos, and garden tours helped to create an educational initiative that reached several thousand participants.

Project_Name: Everglades Oyster Reef Restoration - Phase II
Project_Description: Phase II of the Everglades Oyster Reef Restoration project created 10 oyster reefs in the Caloosahatchee River, Estero Bay and Henderson Creek estuaries. In addition, this project initiated an oyster shell recycling program, an oyster gardening program, and created an oyster hatchery to seed future reef sites with local oyster spat to accelerate reef growth.
Restoration_Technique: oyster gardening, oyster reef construction, species enhancement

Project_Name: Wildcat Cove Salt Marsh Restoration
Project_Description: This project restored the degraded saltmarsh and mangrove systems of Wildcat Cove Preserve within St. Lucie County, Florida.  This 129-acre site was impounded in the 1960’s for mosquito control purposes.  The Wildcat Cove restoration project reconnected the site to the Indian River Lagoon by removing invasive vegetation and installing six culverts.  This on-the-ground restoration project benefits living marine resources by increasing available habitat that is important to the refuge, spawning, and rearing areas essential to fisheries.  Not only did this project help to stabilize this estuarine system, but it also educated and engaged the local community through native species planting events and educational signage placed throughout the preserve. Approximately 99 acres of saltmarsh and mangrove habitat was restored.
Restoration_Technique: culvert modification (including replacement), invasives removal: vegetation, planting

Project_Name: Matheson Hammock Central Tidal Creek Restoration
Project_Description: With grant funds from NOAA's Community-Based Restoration Program and Fish America Foundation, volunteers from the Wildlife Research Team (WRT) worked to restore tidal flow to mangrove hammock that was choked by downed trees and debris. Matheson Hammock, an 832-acre park in Florida, is home to the last mangrove forest in urban Miami-Dade County. The hammock served as habitat for migratory fish and sea turtles until being devastated by Hurricane Andrew in 1992. WRT volunteers used canoes to carefully remove dead and decayed flora and non-native species such as Australian pine, restoring 23 acres of mangrove habitat.
Restoration_Technique: debris removal, tide gate modification (including replacement)

Project_Name: Florida Keys Diadema and Coral Reef Restoration - Phase II
Project_Description: The goal of this project was to locate areas where Diadema urchin juveniles are settling in the Florida Keys, yet have a low chance of survivorship due to unstable substrate, and relocate them to more stable areas where their grazing activities may benefit the coral reef.  Unfortunately, three hurricanes impacted the Florida Keys during the grant and urchins did not survive in the unstable areas.  It was, therefore, not possible to successfully complete the project by relocating urchins and monitoring effects on the coral reef.  However, after the close of this grant, a large number of juvenile urchins did recruit in 2006 and TNC partnered with the Marine Sanctuary and local volunteers to relocate some of these animals.

Project_Name: Tampa Bay Oil Spill - Ft. DeSoto Dune Restoration
Project_Description: Two boardwalks were constructed in order to decrease the amount of harmful foot traffic through the dunes in an effort to increase the amount of sand on the beach.
Species_Benefited: (Turtle, green sea - Florida Breeding Populations - Endangered), (Turtle, kemp's ridley sea - Range-wide - Endangered), (Turtle, loggerhead sea - Range-wide - Threatened)

Project_Name: Tampa Bay Oil Spill - Treasure Island Dune Vegetation Restoration
Project_Description: A series of beach dunes was created and planted with native dune vegetation.  A beach dune walkover was also  incorporated to protect the developing dunes.
Species_Benefited: (Turtle, green sea - Florida Breeding Populations - Endangered), (Turtle, loggerhead sea - Range-wide - Threatened), (Turtle, olive ridley sea - Range-wide - Threatened)

Project_Name: Long Term Assessment of Seagrass Restoration in Tampa Bay I & II
Project_Description: Successfully transplanted seagrass beds have been demonstrated to provide many of the same functional and structural characteristics of natural conditions.  However, information concerning how to assess and conduct a successful seagrass restoration is limited. This project 'Long Term Assessment of Seagrass Restoration' is a continuation of a program established by the State of Florida in 2002 dedicated to improving the evaluation of restoration success.  This monitoring effort was accomplished by providing an assessment of the seagrass planted in the first three years of the project, as well as monitoring a long term seagrass restoration project approximately 20 years old.  Lessons learned and seagrass restoration recommendations from this project were disseminated to benefit natural resource decision makers.

Project_Name: Florida's Bay Scallop Metapopulation Stabilization
Project_Description: At one time, populations of bay scallops flourished along the Gulf coast of Florida.  Unfortunately, today bay scallops are found only in isolated populations along the coast and they are struggling to recover.  Studies have shown that many populations have poor recovery potential because scallop larvae do not survive to reproduce.  With this in mind, the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission designed an innovative restoration project that hatchery-reared and released scallop larvae at several sites to help rebuild the populations.
Lead_Implementer: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission

Project_Name: FISH Preserve Habitat Restoration Project
Project_Description: The Florida Institute of Saltwater Heritage (FISH) restored approximately 24.5 acres of mangrove, wetlands, and upland habitat within the FISH Preserve in Manatee County, Florida.  FISH is dedicated to the promotion and preservation of the cultural and environmental integrity of Florida's traditional maritime communities.  In 2000 FISH was able to acquire 95 acres of coastal habitat adjacent to the Village of Cortez and Sarasota Bay and called it the FISH Preserve.  This restoration project restored tidal circulation to the preserve, removed invasive species and planted native vegetation to restore important fish habitat.
Restoration_Technique: debris removal, invasives removal: vegetation, planting

Project_Name: Feather Sound Seagrass Recovery Project
Project_Description: The Feather Sound Seagrass Recovery Project was a multiphase, multi-agency research project to identify the potential causes of poor seagrass recovery in the Feather Sound region of Old Tampa Bay.  During Phase 1 (2002-2003) the research team identified several potential causes of poor seagrass recovery, including poorer water quality than the other three quadrants sampled in Old Tampa Bay; slower circulation and flushing; epiphyte loading; and hydrogen sulfide toxicity.  The information collected in Phase 1 then became the foundation for the second phase of the project (2004 - 2007) to develop a management strategy to address the causes for slow seagrass recovery in Feather Sound. Data and analysis for Phase 2 was completed in 2006. An essential component of this project was development of management recommendations for the Feather Sound area.

Project_Name: Water Environment Leadership Program
Project_Description: The University of South Florida developed and hosted the Community Water leadership Program, a series of six sessions designed to educate community elected officials, governmental employees and community leaders.  These workshops were hosted to empower Tampa Bay's leaders and decision makers with a solid base of knowledge in the areas of natural resource conservation, restoration, and enhancement as they connect with water resources.  In addition, more than 200 participants attended a one day Water Rally conference in March of 2006 designed to provide another forum for discussion on the topic of water policy and conservation opportunities in the Tampa Bay area.

Project_Name: Clearwater Marine Aquarium Environmental Education Booklets
Project_Description:
The Clearwater Marine Aquarium developed and printed 12,500 books titled "Winter, the Dolphin who lost her tail".  This dolphin was injured due to marine-debris and provided the aquarium the perfect platform for an education and outreach initiative built around marine conservation and protection, dolphin biology and behavior, and the importance of healthy marine environments.  The Clearwater Marine Aquarium provided more than 220 presentations to local schools, camps and events to educate the community.  The book can be found at
www.winterstail.com.

Project_Name: Youth for a Change II
Project_Description: The Suncoast Earth Force 'Youth for a Change' program was an educational initiative to help teachers and students connect with their watersheds.  Through this program, educators received the necessary training and resources needed to incorporate effective hands-on environmental lessons in their classrooms.  Through a professional development program, Earth Force taught 20 local educators how to teach students to contribute to the preservation and conversation of their local watershed through creative and sustainable solutions.  Projects implemented through 15 schools included a focus on a variety of topics: manatees, invasive species, water conservation, water quality, bird sanctuary, wetlands, butterfly gardens, tree planting, the watershed, and recycling of ink cartridges, cell phones, and paper.

Project_Name: Pinellas County Classroom Teacher Environmental Grants - Phase II
Project_Description: The Pinellas Education Foundation has developed the Teach for Excellence mini-grant program to encourage teachers to develop and implement innovative classroom projects that lead to the protection and conservation of the Florida ecosystem.  Through a competitive process, three schools were selected by the Foundation to receive funding.  Each school developed their own project goals, timelines and methodologies to enhance the environmental education of that school.

Project_Name: Lignumvitae Key Seagrass Restoration
Project_Description: Approximately 1.0 acre of prop scars and blowouts from boat groundings were restored at 6 different sites using fill and bird stakes.

Project_Name: Cargill Park Salt Marsh Planting
Project_Description: NOAA's Community-based Restoration Program, Restore America's Estuaries and Fish America Foundation partnered with Tampa Bay Watch to fund salt marsh restoration at multiple sites around Tampa Bay.  26 volunteers from Cargill Fertilizer, Inc. participated in planting 2,000 plugs of marsh grass the shoreline at Cargill and Williams Parks. These grasses provide nursery habitat for important fishery species and also protect the shoreline from erosion.

Project_Name: Cockroach Bay Tidal Creek Marsh Planting
Project_Description: The Cockroach Bay Braided Tidal Creek project created a new 15 acre coastal wetland system, ready for planting in fall 2004.  Several large community salt marsh planting events will create 10 acres of salt marsh wetlands.

Project_Name: Little Bird Key Salt Marsh and Oyster Restoration
Project_Description: Through funding provided by a partnership between NOAA's Community-based Restoration Program and Restore America's Estuaries, Tampa Bay Watch restored approximately .15 acres of salt marsh and created .2 acres of oyster reef  near Little Bird Key bird rookery in Boca Ciega Bay, near St. Petersburg, Florida. Little Bird Key is an important National Wildlife Refuge and breeding ground for colonial bird species.

Project_Description: Four reefs were constructed at each of three sites, for a total of 12 reefs.  Four different materials were used to create reefs at each of the sites and consisted of fossilized shell, crushed concrete, crushed limestone and polypropylene Seawall Reefs.

Project_Name: Restoration of Intertidal Reefs in Mosquito Lagoon, Florida
Project_Description: The goal of this project was to implement a scientifically-based restoration technique that minimizes wake damage from recreational vessels on intertidal reefs of the eastern oyster Crassostrea virginica.  Oyster mats were placed in the intertidal area to establish new substrates for oyster settlement.  Leveling of existing dead oyster reefs and the placement of seagrass plugs was tested as potential techniques for increasing oyster settlement and survival.

Project_Name: Ding Darling National Wildlife Refuge Mangrove Recovery Project
Project_Description: Through a partnership with the Fish America Foundation and the NOAA Restoration Center, the International Federation of Fly Fishers (FFF) and the US Fish and Wildlife Service implemented the first phase of a comprehensive restoration of mangrove estuary systems devastated by hurricane effects and impacted by human development. The first phase of the comprehensive effort focused on invasive plant management, habitat assessment, and hurricane damage restoration at Ding Darling National Wildlife Refuge on Sanibel Island, Florida. This project restored 3.27 acres of mangrove habitat.
Restoration_Technique: debris removal, invasives removal: vegetation, planting
Lead_Implementer: Federation of Fly Fishers, US Fish and Wildlife Service

Project_Name: Northwest Florida Oyster Restoration
Project_Description: The Northwest Florida Oyster Restoration Project initiated a collaborative program to salvage shell materials from local restaurants and established six oyster reef habitats over three counties in northwest Florida (Escambia, Santa Rosa, and Okaloosa Counties). A total of 0.75 acres of oyster habitat were restored through this program with the assistance of 75 volunteers and 1200 volunteer hours. This will help many aspects of coastal shorelines, including improving water quality conditions, reducing sedimentation and lessening the impact of catastrophic storm events.

Project_Name: Staghorn Coral Restoration in the Florida Keys using Reef Resilience Principles
Project_Description: The objectives of this effort were to build 125 staghorn coral colonies from 25 wild colonies and then transplant these propagates to sites within the Upper Keys to restore degraded reefs.
Species_Benefited: (Coral, staghorn - Caribbean and Western Atlantic - Threatened)

Project_Name: Munisport Landfill Superfund Site - Biscayne Bay Mangrove Restoration
Project_Description: Approximately 75 acres of mangrove habitat were restored within the Biscayne Bay estuary, and tidal influence was reestablished by breaching an existing dike and modifying existing culverts.

Project_Name: Environmental Distance Learning Project IV
Project_Description: The Environmental Distance Learning Program was a web-based educational initiative that delivered real time (virtual field trip) experience of area ecosystems to educators and students.  This was accomplished through a network of remote field sensor stations, satellite, and GIS technology that supplied the water, weather, and visual data that was incorporated into the curriculum of classrooms throughout the Pinellas County school system.  More than 500 teachers participated in a formal training to learn how to bring this program back to their classrooms.

Project_Name: Boca Ciega Bay Scallop Restoration Project
Project_Description: This restoration project was designed as the first step to reestablish Bay Scallop populations (Argopecten irradians) within Boca Ciega Bay using an innovative stock enhancement strategy.   This strategy involved the release of hatchery reared reproductively mature larvae into containment booms within two sites in Boca Ciega Bay.  The booms were used to prevent excessive dispersal of the scallops to help increase abundance to a density where the population can become more stable and self sustaining.  This project successfully demonstrated that the strategy of releasing late-stage pediveliger larvae resulted in the recruitment of juvenile scallops to artificial collectors and seagrass habitat at two restoration sites: Tarpon Key and Mullet Key Bayou.

Project_Name: A.J. Palonis Park Marsh Restoration
Project_Description: Tampa Bay Watch planted smooth cord grass landward of some recently created oyster reefs to restore approximately .5 acres of Tampa Bay Shoreline.

Project_Name: Port Redwing Tidal Pond Restoration- Phase II
Project_Description: Volunteers and school groups will replant one acre of shoreline along the Shultz Nature Preserve that has show less success than surrounding areas.  They will also monitor the site to determine success for one year.

Project_Name: Ft. DeSoto Park Oyster Restoration
Project_Description: Tampa Bay Watch worked the Pinellas County Parks Department and local volunteers to create over an acre of oyster reef along the campground shoreline.

Project_Description: Tampa Bay Watch worked with the Suncoast Seabird Sanctuary to restore 0.1 acres of oyster reef around this colonial nesting bird island.

Project_Name: Tampa Shoreline Iniitative II
Project_Description: The Mayor's Beautification Program conducted Phase II of the 'Tampa Shoreline Restoration Initiative', a community-based project that supported habitat restoration projects across 6 sites within the City of Tampa.  This project completed the Shoreline Tracking and Reporting System, as well as the Tampa Shoreline Restoration Initiative Master Plan.  Both tools will be instrumental in future restoration design and planning for the City of Tampa.  More than 2,000 volunteers participated in close to 80 individual conservation and restoration projects during this project.  In total more than 12,000 native plants were installed and approximately 6.5 acres of coastal habitat were restored.

Project_Name: Southern Tampa Bay Habitat Education
Project_Description: The "Habitat Education on Southern Tampa Bay" project led by Around the Bend Nature Tours provided the opportunity for 1,997 students from Manatee County Schools to participate in 50 field trips to Emerson Point, Rye Wilderness, Manatee River and Durante Parks.  These field trips provided the opportunity for the students to participate in hands-on education and restoration activities.  Students participated in fun projects focused on the identification and eradication of a variety of invasive exotic vegetation within the parks.  In addition, the field trip curriculum covered a nature walk where the topics of biodiversity, habitat conservation, and restoration were discussed.

Project_Description: The Pinellas Education Foundation is continuing the Teach for Excellence mini-Grant program, for the third year in a row, to encourage teachers to use their imaginations for developing creative projects.  All of the potential mini-grant projects would help to enhance the environmental education of the community. Each project will be unique in its goals, methodology, and timeline.

Project_Name: Tampa Bay Living Legacy Documentary Film
Project_Description: The documentary film "Tampa Bay: Living Legacy", created by the Tampa Bay Estuary Program, spans a half-century of transformations in Tampa Bay's evolution and seeks to educate the public about the Tampa Bay watershed and involve citizens in activities that help to improve and restore Tampa Bay.  The story is told, in part, through interviews with elected officials, scientists, and citizen advocates.  The film provides practical information on ways everyone can help protect Florida's largest open-water estuary.  Aired on two regional PBS stations and in interviews on National Public Radio, this film is estimated to have reached more than 100,000 households and it is hoped that it will continue to help instill a sense of stewardship and personal responsibility for the bay's welfare.

Project_Name: Florida Aquarium Stormwater Education Program
Project_Description: This project created and implemented a stormwater education project for middle and high school students, science teachers, and the general public that visit the Florida Aquarium.  The education program included removal of invasive plants at the stormwater pond, construction of an observation platform overlooking the site, curriculum development and implementation for students and public programs, and creation of teachers workshops. This project created formal and informal educational opportunities on the impact of human activities on stormwater runoff and how they affect Tampa Bay.

Project_Name: Protecting Bird Colonies Through Strategic Partnerships - Phase II
Project_Description: Audubon of Florida initiated Phase II of this project to ensure the protection of colonial waterbird populations.  The project surveyed 43 nesting colonies which benefited 30 waterbird species within the Tampa Bay area. The project focused on species management and monitoring, conservation and educational outreach, habitat and ecosystem protection and restoration.  Project partners posted signage at 22 colonies, participated in 13 habitat restoration projects, and led multiple education and outreach events.

Project_Name: Tampa Bay Bird Conservation Partnership
Project_Description: The 'Tampa Bay Bird Conservation Partnership' will work to improve habitat protection on three National Wildlife Refuge (NWR) sites: Passage Key, Egmont Key and Pinellas NWR.  This project is part of the ongoing refuge system effort to educate the public and increase awareness and appreciation of wildlife resources and conservation.  Outreach material will address information about the refuges, hazards of monofilament and marine debris, threats to nesting habitats, and threats to wildlife.  Sanctuary signage will be posted on two of the refuges and boundary signage will be posted on all three refuge sites.  It is expected that wildlife interpretive exhibits will be established inside the newly renovated guardhouse building on Egmont Key and habitat restoration efforts will be implemented by treating 100 acres of Brazilian Pepper and removing 300 Australian pine trees on Egmont Key and Pinellas Islands.
Restoration_Technique: bird habitat enhancement, invasives removal: vegetation

Educators implemented projects at 18 schools across the Tampa Bay area focused on a variety of topics ranging from reducing trash and pollution to restoring a campus pond, expanding a wetland, xeriscaping, invasive species identification and removal, water conservation, water quality, gardening, and wildlife conservation.

Project_Name: Tampa Bay Wetland Restoration Assessment

Information gained through this project was distributed to resource managers through a project report, oral and poster presentations at national and regional conferences, and thesis defense and manuscript completion.

The project was conducted at Andrew's Island, a mangrove-covered island in northern Boca Ciega Bay, St. Petersburg, Florida, and it helped to restore lost oyster reefs, reduce erosion along the shoreline, improve water quality, and enhance habitat for fish and wildlife.

Project_Name: Indian River Lagoon Hard Clam Restoration
Project_Description: In the last 50 years wild harvest of the Indian River Lagoon hard clam (Mercenaria mercenaria) population sustained a major fishery. Today, however, that same population has been depleted as a commercial fishery for over a decade. Scientists at the FL Fish and Wildlife Research Institute have worked to collaborate with other scientists, fishermen, and aquaculture industries to investigate restoration options. Two methods of enhancement were implemented: 1) immediate free-release of fertilized larvae and 2) delayed controlled-release of ready-to-set pediveligers. Assessment of these restoration methods were variable in their success, but results indicate that the amount of hard clam larvae within the target basin increased after larval release events; adult densities remained consistent; and spawner clumps were present.  Results suggest that settlement issues exist, and the project team intends to continue developing abilities to research and restore IRL hard clam populations.
Lead_Implementer: Florida Fish and Wildlife Research Institute

This process will occur in three different sub-regions of the Florida Reef Tract (Lower Keys, Miami transition, and Broward).  Sub-regional and sub-zonal variation in survivorship and growth will be monitored.
Lead_Implementer: The Nature Conservancy of the Florida Keys

The creation of oyster bars and planting of marsh grasses helped stabilize the island and allowed for the expansion of the salt marsh. Approximately 33 volunteers contributed nearly 190 hours toward restoration of this island.

Funding for this project was provided through a partnership between NOAA's Community-based Restoration Program and Restore America's Estuaries.

Project_Name: Whale Island Salt Marsh Restoration

More than 30 volunteers contributed 112 hours to plant the grasses grown by the high school nurseries. This project was funded through a partnership between NOAA's Community-based Restoration Program and Restore America's Estuaries.

Project_Name: Weedon Island Preserve Oyster Restoration
Project_Description: Tampa Bay Watch worked with volunteers to construct three shoreline fringing reefs to provide substrate for oysters and protect the eroding shoreline on Weedon Island in St. Petersburg, Florida. This 3,700 acre coastal preserve situated on Old Tampa Bay contains several different aquatic and upland ecosystems, including mangrove forests, pine flatwoods and oak hammoks.  Volunteers constructed three oyster reef bars adjacent to the shoreline to absorb the wave energy. In addition to shoreline protection, the reef will also provide fishery habitat and filter the water in the Bay. Funding for this project was provided through a partnership between NOAA's Community-based Restoration Program and Restore America's Estuaries.

Project_Name: Deadman's Island Restoration Project
Project_Description:

native oyster, Crassostrea virginica, habitat which has also declined. A solution to address the 
habitat erosion is to build a wave break (energy dissipater) for the barrier island. This natural oyster 
shell wave break called Ecodiscs will increase the native oyster habitat by providing a foundation 
for a natural oyster reef

This project utilized the offshore placement of artificial vertical oyster reef structures along shoreline to reduce wave energy and placed material to plant emergent salt marsh.

Project_Name: Seeding of Eyed Oyster Larvae onto Recycled Shell Reefs -- St. Lucie Estuary
Project_Description: The main objective of this project was to create four oyster reefs near the Evans-Crary Bridge in the St. Lucie Estuary (SLE) in Stuart, FL and two control oyster reefs in Indian River Lagoon (IRL) in Ft. Along with restoring oyster reefs and their associated species, the project enabled us to determine if this restoration approach would work in an area where oysters and their substrate have been completely obliterated with little or no available seed source.

Project_Name: Seeding of Eyed Oyster Larvae onto Recycled Shell Reefs -- Ft. Pierce IRL
Project_Description: Tremendous losses of oyster reefs had occurred in the St. Lucie River Estuary due to physical changes to the watershed, pollution, erosion and hurricanes. The main objective of this project was to create four oyster reefs near the Evans-Crary Bridge in the St. Lucie Estuary (SLE) in Stuart, FL (see RCDB #2487) and two control oyster reefs in Indian River Lagoon (IRL) in Ft. Pierce, FL.  Two of the reefs in the SLE and one reef in the IRL were seeded with oyster larvae inside containment booms to jumpstart their propagation.  The seeding of these reefs helped to create a more stable seed source.  Along with restoring oyster reefs and their associated species, the project enabled us to determine if this restoration approach would work in an area where oysters and their substrate have been completely obliterated with little or no available seed source. Benefits of the project beyond the restored oyster reef include improved water quality, increased public awareness of oyster reefs and their value to aquatic ecosystems, shoreline stabilization and improvement in fisheries habitat.

Project_Name: M/V Anzhela Explorer - Coral Reef Restoration
Project_Description:
The Anzhela Explorer, a 78 foot steel-hulled motorized catamaran, sank off the coast of southeast Florida adjacent to Golden Beach, Miami-Dade County on 26 March 2007. The vessel initially sank on the shallow, nearshore reef and was then pushed shoreward across the reef a distance of approximately 366 meters, by the very rough seas that were occurring at the time of the sinking. As a result of the vessel sinking, extensive physical (fractured and gouged reef structure), and biological (broken and dislodged reef biota including hard and soft corals and sponges) injuries occurred on the reef. The initial triage and salvage of living hard and soft corals was conducted during 29 March-1 May 2007, with subsequent reattachment of the organisms during early June 2007. This work was conducted by a team comprised of local, state and federal diving scientists.

The second phase of the restoration plan included the management and stabilization of the significant amount of rubble material created as a result of the vessel grounding. The State trustees contracted with Sea Byte Inc. to conduct the rubble related portions of the restoration effort.Work related to rubble stabilization was conducted on the injury site in two phases. The initial phase consisted of a mapping and rubble collection effort and the second phase consisted of rubble stabilization and habitat reconstruction effort.

Project_Name: Tampa Bay Seagrass Transplanting Project
Project_Description: The purpose of this project was to restore seagrass in areas of Hillsborough Bay where they have existed historically. Manatee grass was transplanted from a permitted donor site by staff, students and 53 community volunteers, who dedicated over 300 hours to the project. After one year, the project demonstrated that not only had the 1,200 m² transplanted manatee grass been restored to the area, but that it expanded beyond the initial planting site, resulting in approximately 2,800m² of restored seagrass beds.  Many fish and shellfish species will benefit from the restored habitat and water quality improvements are expected on continue due to the expansion of the seagrass beds. Project_Name: St. Lucie Estuary Oyster Reef Habitat Restoration Project
Project_Description:
The purpose of the St. Lucie Estuary (SLE) Oyster Reef Habitat Restoration Project is to restore historic oyster reef habitat and improve shoreline stability. By restoring approximately 2 acres of oyster reef habitat, and creating stretches of living shoreline, in the SLE, the project furthers the Estuary Restoration Act's mission to protect and restore marine and coastal habitats.  The project also furthers NOAA’s coastal resiliency objectives due to the fact that oyster reef restoration combined with living shorelines can help to protect against stresses caused by sea level rise/climate change.  

By leveraging the ERA funds with St. Lucie River Issues Team grant funds, the County was able to increase the constructed oyster reef acreage to 4.52 acres during the summer of 2013. The living shoreline component of oyster shell bags, oyster domes and saltmarsh planting was completed early summer 2014.  959 volunteers contributed 2133 hours to the living shoreline component of the project.  This project will post-restoration monitoring efforts through the fall of 2017.

Project_Description: Tampa Bay Watch implemented two community-based oyster restoration projects as part of the Community Oyster Reef Enhancement (CORE) Program. Project_Description:
Since the 1980’s, oyster reef habitat has declined precipitously in Florida’s Big Bend region of the Gulf of Mexico. To mitigate these declines, this oyster restoration project incorporated two new techniques in oyster restoration: (1) use of bagged building blocks of living oysters transplanted to create instant living reefs that are resilient to wave action, and (2) designing reefs to capture and protect extant oyster spat and increase growth and survival by enhancing water flow around reef structure in a way that allows built reefs to naturally expand.

The restoration project established stable substrate along 25 km of shoreline and used donated, bagged live oysters to boost oyster recruitment. Clean limerock boulders established a hard substrate over existing eroded sand bars and each site was lined with the oyster bags. 

The restoration of reefs in this pilot project suggests that long term resilience can be built into oyster reefs by the addition of hardened surface and durable substrate and that the established artificial reefs have positive effects on erosion, water flow, water quality, and wildlife.

Project_Name: North Peninsula State Park Saltmarsh Restoration
Project_Description:
This project restored and enhanced approximately 9 acres of estuarine saltmarsh within the North Peninsula State Park in northeast Florida.
The project provided direct restoration to 2 acres of historic saltmarsh habitat and enhanced an additional 7 acres of habitat that was filled with spoil during the navigation and dredging of the Intracoastal Waterway back in the 1950s.  This project focused on the removal of exotic invasive species, restoration of the natural wetland elevation of the site, and stabilization of the shoreline edge habitat through planting of low marsh vegetation.  The project also provided nursery habitat benefits to a variety of commercially and recreationally important fisheries species, as well as numerous other estuarine organisms.
Restoration_Technique: fill removal, invasives removal: vegetation, planting

Project_Name: Threatened Coral Recovery and Restoration Phase IV_Florida
Project_Description: The Nature Conservancy (TNC) and project partners built upon Acropora coral recovery and restoration work that was piloted with TNC-NOAA Community-based Habitat Restoration Grant Program (CRP) support beginning in 2004.  This project was scaled up dramatically with American Recovery and Reinvestment Act (ARRA) funding provided by NOAA’s Restoration Center in 2009.  The project capitalized on these previous efforts by maintaining a minimum of 10,000 corals in established nurseries managed by TNC and its partners, and outplanting 8,000 additional corals to degraded reefs over two years.  By building on work previously supported by NOAA, this project will contribute significantly to the recovery of federally listed staghorn coral (Acropora cervicornis) and elkhorn coral (Acropora palmata) and restoration of some of America’s most significant coral reefs.  Additionally, acroporid corals provide structural complexity that is important to many commercially and recreationally important fish species (Bruckner, 2002) so by restoring them the project will also help enhance the fisheries and tourism-based economies that they support.  The project was implemented in 8 subregions of the Florida and USVI reef systems, with nursery and restoration sites located in each subregion.  See map for St. Thomas and St. Croix records.
Restoration_Technique: coral nursery, coral reattachment, coral reef construction
Lead_Implementer: The Nature Conservancy, Florida and Caribbean Chapter

Project_Name: Florida Keys Shallow Sponge Restoration Phase II
Project_Description: We have expanded a past NOAA-TNC Community Restoration Project to increase our restoration footprint and better assess the restoration of hard-bottom sponge communities. We have: (a) added more restoration sites, (b) broadened the taxonomic diversity of sponges on restoration sites, and (c) expanded our monitoring beyond measures of sponge transplant success to include assessment of the restoration of ecological function, especially as essential nursery habitat for fish and invertebrates. We also will explore the potential for the restoration of reef-dwelling sponges in a preliminary study in collaboration with NOAA supported scientists working on coral restoration along the Florida Keys reef tract.

Project_Name: Mosquito Lagoon Marine Discovery Center Marsh Restoration
Project_Description: The St. Johns River Water Management District worked with partners such as the Marine Discovery Center and the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission to complete excavation, grading, planting and other tasks needed for the construction/restoration of the salt marsh nursery at the Mosquito Lagoon Marine Enhancement Center located at a former high school in New Smyrna Beach, Florida.
