Project_Name: Indian River Lagoon Impoundment Reconnection and Restoration
Project_Description: The St. John River Water Management District worked with the Brevard County Mosquito Control District and the Merritt Island National Wildlife Refuge to install culverts to enhance fish habitat in Brevard County, FL.  At the Sykes Creek Impoundments (C-2 North and C-2 South), which comprise nearly 2,015 acres of wetland, 17 culverts were installed to recreate flow where natural creek mouths previously existed and provide fish with access to habitat.  Work began on this component in September of 2015, restoring 1,289 acres.  The balance of acreage was completed in the fall of 2015.  Additional work was implemented in other impoundments within the Merritt Island National Wildlife Refuge to address subsidence. Subsidence has reduced sediment levels to elevations too low to support marsh grass or mangrove habitat.  This component of the project was implemented first as a pilot project to evaluate a variety of methods to bring subsided areas up to an appropriate elevation to support vegetation typical of wetlands in the area.  The pilot effort was completed in the spring of 2016.  Project results led to implementation of an expanded effort in the fall of 2016/winter of 2017.  Final planting was completed December 2017.
Restoration_Technique: berm/dike removal, culvert modification (including replacement), placement of fill/dredge material, research/recommendations/surveys

Project_Name: Upper Florida Keys Coral Population Enhancement through Active Propagation - CRF
Project_Description: This project addressed restoration actions to help recover Acropora cervicornis (staghorn coral) and A. palmata (elkhorn coral), two coral species that are listed as “Threatened” under the Endangered Species Act.   Staghorn (9,925) and elkhorn (4,100) corals were transplanted from Coral Reef Foundation nurseries to reefs at densities and sizes that exceed what is found within the natural population.  Relatively large corals (>25cm to 45cm diameter) were grown in nurseries and transplanted to various reef sites in the Florida Keys.  Through careful hypothesis-driven monitoring, whether or not clusters and thickets that approximate pre-dieoff densities will be more resilient to existing disturbances was observed. The project also addressed developing offshore nursery techniques for three additional species of stony coral that were listed as threatened under the US Endangered Species Act after the project began (Orbicella annularis, Orbicella faveolata, and Dendrogyra cylindricus).

Project_Description: This project removes spoil sediment placed during the dredging of the Intracoastal Waterway, to re-establish estuarine wetlands on the site. Project_Name: Hydrologic reconnection of the mangrove forest within the southern portion of the Tampa Bay Interbay Peninsula
Project_Description: This project assisted MacDill Air Force Base (AFB) with their ongoing efforts to restore the mangrove forest within the southern portion of the Tampa Bay Interbay Peninsula. The primary restoration objective was to remove spoil mounds, many of which were colonized by non-native vegetation such as Brazilian pepper.  This project expanded the hydro-blasting efforts to additional locations within the project site and included the removal of an additional 50 mounds to improve the hydrological conditions within the mangrove system.  In addition to benefits to the mangroves, a variety of estuarine dependent fauna also benefited from the enhancement of the mangroves including: common snook, red drum, sheepshead, mullet, oysters and blue crab.

Project_Name: Mulberry Mangrove/Tidal Creek Project and Lewis Lake Project
Project_Description: On December 7, 1997, over 50 million gallons of acidic process water was released into the Alafia River from a fertilizer plant in Mulberry, Polk County, Florida. The release injured natural resources in the Alafia River and in Tampa Bay. Several public agencies, including NOAA, FDEP and EPC, worked together to assess natural resource injuries and losses caused by the Spill and to recover natural resource damages to compensate for these losses from the party responsible. This project consisted of two components implemented on MacDill Airforce Base: the Mangrove/Tidal Creek project and the Lewis Lake Project.  The first component involved the restoration of 34 acres of intertidal lagoons/channels, high and low marsh platforms, mangrove islands, upland islands, upland hammocks, and relic mangrove forest. To accomplish project goals, large stands of non-native vegetation had to be removed, followed by excavation of lagoons and channels to restore tidal availability. The second component, the Lewis Lake Project, modified an existing freshwater/oligohaline stormwater treatment pond that was intermittently intertidal via the pond’s overflow control structure. This 26.6 acre project increased the size of the pond, created new open water and marsh platforms, removed all cattails and other nuisance/non-native plants from marsh platforms, and resulted in improved water quality for the bay due to enhanced stormwater treatment capacity of the pond.
Restoration_Technique: fill removal, invasives removal: vegetation, planting
Lead_Implementer: Southwest Florida Water Management District-S.W.I.M. Program

Project_Name: Mulberry Shoreline Stabilization and Enhancement through Oyster Reef Construction at MacDill Air Force Base
Project_Description: On December 7, 1997, over 50 million gallons of acidic process water was released into the Alafia River from a fertilizer plant in Mulberry, Polk County, Florida (the Spill). The release injured natural resources in the Alafia River and in Tampa Bay. Several public agencies, including NOAA, FDEP and EPC, worked together to assess natural resource injuries and losses caused by the Spill and to recover natural resource damages to compensate for these losses from the party responsible. The 'Shoreline Stabilization and Enhancement through Oyster Reef Construction at MacDill Air Force Base' project was selected to compensate the public for injured natural resources.  Phases IV and V of a multi-phase project were implemented in partnership with Tampa Baywatch. In Phase IV approximately 3,250 shell bags were deployed by volunteers to create ~2,250 sq. ft. of oyster reef.  In addition, Phase V deployed 1,781 oyster domes restoring ~7,124 sq. ft of oyster reef.

Project_Name: Mulberry Oyster Reef Creation in Hillsborough Bay
Project_Description:
A phosphogypsum stack breached at the MPI phosphoric acid and fertilizer production facility in Mulberry, Polk County, Florida on December 7, 1997. Around 50-56 million gallons of acidic process water flowed into the Alafia River and caused a fish kill in the Alafia River, damaged shoreline and upland vegetation in some areas within Polk County, and caused losses of palustrine and estuarine resource services.

The Restoration Council was formed with representation from NOAA, the FDEP and the EPC, and they jointly developed a Final Damage Assessment and Restoration Plan and Environmental Assessment. Settlement monies administered through NOAA funded the project design and implementation of an oyster reef restoration project. NOAA selected the Tetra Tech team in May 2013 to provide the engineering, environmental, geotechnical, and implementation services for the project.

The Project was permitted for 28,350 square feet (0.65 acre) of reef substrate. The total installed reef area was 21,470 square feet (0.49 acre) or 76% of the permitted reef area. The project was installed over 45 days between April 20 and June 24, 2015. A Trustee inspection on June 25, 2015 documented macroalgal and diverse invertebrate colonization of the newly installed reefs.

Project_Name: Indian River Lagoon Preserve State Park Impoundment Restoration
Project_Description: The Indian River Lagoon Impoundment Reconnection and Restoration project was implemented within the Indian River Lagoon Preserve State Park in Brevard County, Florida.  The project reconnected impounded marshes completely enclosed by a series of dikes originally created for mosquito control. The 15-acre impoundment area had an exterior dike, an interior dike, and a dike/ditch system along its upland edge. This project removed the interior dike to restore wetland area and the upland dike to allow a more natural upland transition recreating a path for the “up slope” migration of the wetland with sea level rise. The transitional area was also planted.  Project began construction in summer of 2016.
Restoration_Technique: berm/dike removal, culvert modification (including replacement), fill removal, invasives removal: vegetation
Lead_Implementer: St. Johns River Water Management District

Project_Name: Lemon Creek Wetland Restoration Project
Project_Description: The Lemon Creek Wetland Restoration Project was implemented within the Charlotte Harbor Watershed in Englewood, Florida. The Lemon Bay Conservancy, in partnership with the Southwest Florida Water Management District, restored an abandoned 80-acre golf course now known as Wildflower Preserve. Project_Name: Buildling Coral Resilience through Restoration in Miami-Dade County, Florida
Project_Description: The project conducted coral restoration on nearshore reef habitats of Miami-Dade County, research about resilient coral strains and outreach . More than 12,000 staghorn corals were grown in ocean-based nurseries and outplanted to 7 restoration sites. Experiments that were conducted to identify differences in bleaching resistance in staghorn coral found significant differences among the strains tested and that corals with resistance to bleaching were those that came from locations with historically higher sea water temperatures. A new method was tested to “stress harden” staghorn coral using sub-lethal bleaching to be used for restoration and for increased resilience to climate change, but no benefit in terms of increased thermal tolerance was documented for this species. The number of coral species grown within nurseries in Miami-Dade County and restored on reefs was increased by expanding the culture of 5 species. An outreach and education program was developed to engage the public in coastal resilience, climate change impacts, and coral reef conservation and restoration. The Rescue a Reef program and Reef Futures lab reached 10,000s of members of the public at the Miami Seaquarium, Science Barge, and FROST Science Museum, local science fairs, concerts, and art shows, public seminars and workshops, and through social and conventional media. Over 3,500 of the staghorn corals were planted by citizen scientists, providing significant public match for our activities.
Restoration_Technique: coral nursery, coral reef construction, education and outreach, research/recommendations/surveys, species enhancement

Project_Name: Oyster Reef Restoration in Naples Bay, Florida
Project_Description: Naples, Florida is a highly urbanized low-lying coastal city with extensive infrastructure vulnerable to coastal zone pressures such as extreme high tides and storm surges. The City of Naples will restore 3.6 acres of oyster reefs, increasing coastal resiliency by protecting a mangrove shoreline from storm surge, helping to alleviate storm and flooding effects, and restoring vital oyster habitat at two sites in Naples Bay.  The project will take place in two phases: Phase 1 will restore over three acres of oyster reefs in the southern portion of Naples Bay and Phase 2 will restore oyster reefs at a second smaller area in the more northern part of the bay near Rock Creek. Oyster reef restoration will not only protect the mangrove fringe and attenuate flooding and storm surge effects in the bay, but also will allow for seagrass bed expansion through the creation of suitable protected habitat.

NOAA will work with partners to implement this project to restore 118.2 acres of upland and wetland habitat on fallow degraded farm land recently acquired to expand the Robinson Preserve in the Tampa Bay watershed. NOAA will also work with partners to conduct monitoring of restoration outcomes and outreach and educational activities to share restoration practices and engage stakeholders.
Restoration_Technique: fill removal, placement of fill/dredge material, planting, stream channel reconnection/creation, weir construction
Funding_Program: The RESTORE Act Funds Bucket 2: Comprehensive Plan

Project_Name: Money Bayou Wetlands Restoration
Project_Description: This project is part of the Connecting Coastal Waters (CCW) initiative.  This project will complete planning and design with local partners to, if fully implemented, restore a natural hydrology to approximately 1,000 acres of wetlands on the St. Joseph Bay State Buffer Preserve in Florida. A restoration plan, engineering design, regulatory compliance, monitoring and evaluation plan, and outreach and education plan will be completed to implement this project activity to restore Gulf Coast wetlands in Florida.
Funding_Program: The RESTORE Act Funds Bucket 2: Comprehensive Plan

Project_Name: Florida Keys Coral Restoration Mote CRP 2019
Project_Description: Mote Marine Lab will restore degraded coral reef habitat and promote the recovery of threatened and endangered coral species in the Florida Keys. The project will grow 10,000 corals across five different species each year, and outplant 30,000 corals by securing them to the reef using best management practices for coral restoration. The project will use asexual and innovative sexual production techniques to propagate the corals. 12,000 sexual recruits (400 for each) will be produced for Acropora palmata, Acropora cervicornis, and Orbicella faveolata. The project also includes an ecosystem recovery assessment element that will help the restoration community better understand the full suite of how coral reef ecosystems respond when corals are restored. A Before-After-Control-Impact design will be used to assess coral, fish, and invertebrate cover, abundance, and herbivory rates and identity. The project will test 10 new genotypes for  Acroporid cervicornis and Montastrea cavernosa. The project will also present roughly 300 programs to the public to increase awareness of the Coral Disease Response and Restoration efforts in the FKNMS.
Species_Benefited: (Coral, brain), (Coral, elkhorn - Caribbean and Western Atlantic - Threatened), (Coral, large star), (Coral, mountainous star - Candidate), (Coral, staghorn - Caribbean and Western Atlantic - Threatened)

Project_Name: Florida Keys Mission Iconic Reefs Diadema and Coral Restoration
Project_Description: The Florida Aquarium will use sexual propagation methods to propagate corals in land based nursery and and growout the corals in ocean based nurseries before outplanting to the restoration sites. Over the project 4,250 A. palmata nursery grown corals (~ 12.5 x 12.5 cm or 160 cm2) will be outplanted on 1 m centers using epoxy to help restore 1,785 m2 of A. habitat across Horseshoe and Looe Key reefs. The corals to be outplanted will be a mix of novel genotypes from spawning crosses as well as unique genotypes existing within in-situ nurseries. The proposed project would have a direct and immediate impact over the next three years by outplanting A. palmata colonies representing 165 novel genets at Looe Key and Horseshoe reefs. Diadema urchins will be spawned and cultured at the land based facility until reaching adequate size and to then outplant 10,000 urchins at the selected reef restoration sites. The land based nursery currently houses a broodstock population of 13 adults collected from the Keys. Monitoring will be conducted of both corals and urchins in nursery and at outplanting sites to follow growth and condition.
Restoration_Technique: coral nursery, coral reattachment, coral reef construction, fish hatchery construction, species enhancement

Project_Name: Florida Keys Coral Restoration CRF - 2016
Project_Description:
Funding #NA16NMF4630310, awarded October 2016, supported restoration work along the Florida Reef Tract from Key West through the upper Florida Keys. The restoration efforts under this cooperative agreement were conducted over a three year period (October 1 2016 to September 30 2019) and included several key areas and goals such as:

1) In situ coral nursery development and expansion to accommodate a genetically diverse selection of Acropora corals for restoration. 
2) Support ongoing rescue efforts of Dendrogyra cylindrus and potentially outplant. 
3) Explore opportunities of developing a nursery location outside of Monroe County.
4) Acropora cervicornis (staghorn) restoration targets included: 20 reef sites and 9,000 outplants in total (year 1), 8 reef sites and 8,400 outplants in total (year 2), and 8 reef sites with 12,000 corals outplanted in total (year 3).
5) Acropora palmata (elkhorn) restoration targets included: 5 reef sites and 900 outplants in total (year 1), 8 reef sites and 8,400 outplants in total (year 2), and 8 reef sites with 12,000 corals outplanted in total (year 3).
6) Develop nursery and outplant methods for O. faveolata and O. annularis.
Species_Benefited: (Coral, boulder star - Threatened), (Coral, elkhorn - Caribbean and Western Atlantic - Threatened), (Coral, pillar - Threatened), (Coral, staghorn - Caribbean and Western Atlantic - Threatened), (Coral, star - Threatened)

Project_Name: Florida Keys Coral Restoration CRF - 2019
Project_Description: This will restore degraded coral reef in the Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary.  The proposed project includes three components that together will outplant 84,255 corals on seven reefs across the Florida Reef Tract. The large-scale restoration component will outplant 66,255 corals ( Acropora cervicornis and A. palmata) across three reefs in a manner that meets four (4) of the criteria in the Acropora Recovery Plan. Second, we will engage in pilot projects across four reefs, outplanting a total of 9,000 corals ( Acropora and non- Acropora). The third activity will outplant 9,000 corals from two additional ESA Threatened Species (Orbicella faveolata and O. annularis) . CRF seeks 50% of the restoration project costs from NOAA; CRF will match NOAA funds at 100% and provide additional leveraged funds for project completion.

Project_Name: McCoys Creek Habitat Restoration - Daylighting Phase
Project_Description: McCoys Creek, a tributary of the St. Johns River, is located within the urban landscape of Jacksonville, FL. ln the 1920s, the creek was entirely replaced with straightened ditches and bulkhead canals while the accompanying floodplain and wetlands were filled. In addition, the McCoys channel connection to the St. Johns River has been relocated and buried by an 850-foot culvert. The project partner Groundworks Jacksonville, Inc. intends to create wintering habitat for Atlantic Sturgeon as well as Essential Fish Habitat (EFH) for red drum and lane snapper. The project design will seek to remove the 850 ft. culvert and daylight the stream creating: 4,000 ft. of open channel, 11 acres of  tidal marsh, and 5.5 acres of open water habitat to provide ecological, recreational, and flood mitigation benefits. Planning, engineer work, and permitting will require data collection, modeling, outreach, and other traditional design processes. This project is part of a larger initiative to restore habitat and provide public passive recreational amenities along the 2.8 mile creek. The project is currently at 30% design and will complete 100% design and permitting process during this award period.

Project_Name: Support for Coral Restoration Consortium
Project_Description:
CRF will implement this project by supporting the operational activities of the Coral Restoration Consortium (CRC) in its mission to coordinate dissemination of information within the global coral restoration community. Activities include building platforms for open access data sharing and storage, hosting workshops for the coral community to build and share ideas, and building websites to increase communication. The project will also support the Reef Futures conference series (biennial international conference focused on the practice of coral reef restoration), research and information dissemination of CRC work related to accomplishing its defined priorities, and administration infrastructure support. 

This work provides critical support to the NOAA mission, goals, and priorities including, but not limited to Climate Adaptation and Mitigation, Healthy Oceans, and Resilient Coastal Communities and Economies.

This initial project will conduct design work and permitting for the restoration of 600-hectares of oysters. Up to 100 hectares of oyster habitat will be created in the Pensacola Bay System. The project also includes implementing a living shoreline cost-share program, completing a sediment load assessment study, and designing and permitting restoration of an eroding gully.

Project_Name: Sarasota County Alligator Creek Stream Restoration
Project_Description: The Sarasota County Board of County Commissioners will restore approximately 3.4 miles of Alligator Creek and river bank buffer, totaling 42.8 acres of habitat. Techniques will include water quality improvements, stabilization and naturalization of the existing creek banks, and restoration of historic flood plain areas adjacent to the creek. The restoration will benefit important recreational fish species such as red drum, striped mullet, and snook, and will result in reduced future maintenance costs. This work will also attract more wildlife to the area and increase opportunities for recreation.

Project_Description: Mote Marine Laboratory will restore coral reefs at multiple sites in the Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary including the reefs associated with the Mission: Iconic Reefs effort—an unprecedented, decades-long approach to restore iconic coral reef sites in the sanctuary. Project_Name: Rainwater Preserve Restoration Project
Project_Description: The Nature Conservancy will restore habitat in the Betty and Crawford Rainwater Preserve which was degraded by logging. The preserve contains more than 7.5-river miles and 2,648 acres of habitat along Florida’s western border. The project will help restore natural water flow and allow the return of plant and animal species typically found in longleaf and coastal pine savannahs. Restoration will also include invasive species removal. Project_Description: University of Miami and partners will implement and scale-up strategies to increase the heat tolerance of restored corals, by focusing on corals that survived the summer 2023 heating event and conditioning early life stages of corals to prepare them for warmer temperatures. Project_Name: Indian River Lagoon Habitat Restoration - Riverside Conservancy, Caron Bay, River Breeze Park (Riverside Conservancy)
Project_Description:
This entry is one of 10 project sites included under the name "Indian River Lagoon Habitat Restoration". 

The Indian River Lagoon Council will implement a large-scale restoration in response to an urgent need to restore essential fish habitats, enhance ecosystem functions, and increase resilience in the Indian River Lagoon (IRL) on the Atlantic Coast of Florida.  The overall project design integrates a multi-habitat and multi-site restoration approach that recognizes the complex spatial and temporal diversity of the IRL. The overall project includes a network of 10 discrete project sites and 15 individual projects that cumulatively include restoration and/or enhancement of  seagrass (46 acres), oyster (6.5 acres), saltmarsh wetland (2,125 acres), and living shoreline (6,045 linear feet) habitats.  The project will also re-introduce native clams (21 million) to enhance seagrass habitat.  The ten individual projects will engage the community through site specific outreach events and volunteer opportunities.  
 
This entry includes 3 discrete projects.  Cumulatively, the restoration projects at this site in the Mosquito Lagoon, part of the Indian River Lagoon estuary, include planting 1-acre of seagrass (Halodule wrightii), repatriating 16 million clams over 8 acres, adding fish habitat (artificial reefs) under docks, and  restoring a natural eroding shoreline by restoring 0.2 acre of oyster reef and planting Spartina alterniflora and mangroves, .
Restoration_Technique: oyster reef construction, planting, species enhancement
Species_Benefited: (Clam, hard), (Cordgrass, smooth), (Manatee, west indian - Range-wide - Endangered), (Mangrove, red), (Oyster, eastern), (Shoalgrass)

The overall project design integrates a multi-habitat and multi-site restoration approach that recognizes the complex spatial and temporal diversity of the IRL. The ten individual projects will engage the community through site specific outreach events and volunteer opportunities.  

The Samson Island project in the Banana River, part of the Indian River Lagoon Estuary, is a large scale seagrass and living shoreline project that aims to restore 10 acres of mixed seagrass species and stabilizing 700 linear feet of shoreline. These goals will be achieved by planing 15,000 seagrass planting units and 1,200 mangroves (shoreline).  Wave attenuation devices will also be implemented to reduce energy to aid seagrass recovery.
